title: Stateful SDK Patterns: Cache-aware Quickstart + Runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working draft for a short, opinionated quickstart and runbook aimed at SDK consumers who need to build stateful conversational features (chat history, turns, tool context) while getting the most out of the platform's prefix/KV cache and batching behavior. Goal: reduce latency and token cost by default, surface simple primitives in the SDK for common state patterns, and provide a migration checklist for teams moving from stateless calls to managed state.

Target audience:
- Product engineers adding chat features to a web or mobile app
- Backend engineers building session APIs for multi-turn agents
- SDK maintainers who will implement primitives described here

Assumptions (environment):
- Using Redwood hosted inference or Dedicated with KV/prefix cache enabled
- SDK has access to per-request metadata (session_id, route, model_hint) and client-side checkpoint hooks
- Application can persist small opaque blobs (checkpoint tokens/keys) in a datastore (Redis / DynamoDB)

High-level patterns (short):
1) Stateless + Server-side prefixing (fastest integration path)
   - Send last N user/assistant messages as prompt prefix (truncate smartly)
   - Let Redwood prefix-cache kick in when identical prefixes repeat (e.g., system + static instructions)
   - Use token-level streaming for UI responsiveness

2) KV-checkpointing (recommended for long-lived or high-turn sessions)
   - After each assistant generation, SDK stores a compact KV-checkpoint id returned by Redwood runtime
   - Subsequent requests pass checkpoint_id instead of full history; runtime rehydrates KV cache on the serving node
   - Reduces tokens sent and improves latency for long sessions

3) Hybrid (short prefix + recent messages + KV checkpoint)
   - Send last 2–4 recent messages as explicit prefix to influence immediate local state
   - Provide checkpoint_id to pull the heavy context (long-term facts, memory)

SDK primitives (proposal):
- StatefulSession.create(session_id, opts)
  - opts: { model_hint, fallback_model, ttl_seconds, max_checkpoint_bytes }
  - returns a session handle (local client object) that manages checkpoint refreshes

- session.append(role, text)
  - Buffer messages locally for local echo and to build small prefixes

- session.generate(prompt_overrides, stream_handler?) -> { text, checkpoint_id, telemetry }
  - Accepts short prompt overrides (for local clarifying questions)
  - Handles sending either full prefix or checkpoint_id depending on heuristics and opt-in
  - Returns a new checkpoint_id to persist server-side

- session.restore(checkpoint_id)
  - Lightweight call to rehydrate local session metadata (no tokens charged for checkpoint meta retrieval)

- session.snapshot() -> { checkpoint_blob }
  - For apps that want to store state outside Redwood (e.g., user exports, transfers)

Heuristics (client-side) — when to send full prefix vs checkpoint_id:
- If (turns_since_checkpoint < 3 && total_tokens_sent_last_2_turns < 1024) => send short prefix + checkpoint_id
- If (session_age < 30s) and user hammering UI (rapid keystrokes) => prefer short prefix only for fastest response, then reconcile with checkpoint asynchronously
- If (model_hint changed or system instruction mutated) => send full prefix at least once to establish new cache entry

Recommended default config (SDK opinionated):
- checkpoint_ttl: 7 days (configurable per customer)
- max_checkpoint_blob: 64KB (compressed)
- local_prefix_tokens: 256 tokens (roughly last 3 message pairs)
- aggressive_batch_window: 20ms for UI short requests, 200ms for background actor requests

Quickstart: minimal server flow (30–60m):
1) Create server session endpoint: POST /sessions -> create session in Redis with id, metadata
2) Client attaches session_id to every generate call
3) Use SDK StatefulSession.create(session_id) in backend code
4) On generate: if checkpoint_id exists -> call session.generate({ prompt_overrides }) which will send checkpoint_id + short local prefix
5) Persist returned checkpoint_id to Redis with TTL

Example pseudo-flow (JS sketch):
// server
const session = await sdk.StatefulSession.create(sessionId, { model_hint: 'gpt-like-8k' });
session.append('user', userMessage);
const resp = await session.generate({}, onChunk => clientStream(ws, onChunk));
await persistCheckpoint(sessionId, resp.checkpoint_id); // atomic write

Notes on streaming & checkpoints:
- Stream tokens as soon as runtime emits them (UI snappy). Checkpoints are only returned after generation completes, so UI should optimistically render streamed content and then reconcile if checkpoint-based replay changes anything (rare if deterministic generation).

Telemetry/contract (what SDK emits to Redwood):
- session_id (opaque)
- client_version
- turn_number
- short_prefix_token_count
- used_checkpoint_id (if any)
- model_hint
- latency_ms (client observed)
- failure_mode tag (timeout | mismatch | model-fallback)
Ensure the telemetry payload is small (under 1KB) and tokenized so we can correlate regressions to checkpoint usage.

Edge cases and failure modes (runbook):
- Checkpoint missing on server (404): fallback to full prefix + mark session as "checkpoint cold" and create a new checkpoint after next generation
- Checkpoint too large (413): silently switch to hybrid and memoize that session uses hybrid mode
- Checkpoint stale (TTL expired): try to rehydrate from persisted application-level memory, otherwise prompt user for context (graceful degrade)
- Node mismatch (checkpoint exists but cached on a different zone): try fallback routing policy that prefers rehydration host; if not available, use local prefix and accept cost impact

Migration checklist (from stateless to stateful):
- Audit all generate callsites and ensure session_id propagation (APIs + mobile SDK)
- Add checkpoint persistence with atomic updates
- Add reconciliation steps for streaming vs final checkpoint
- Add observability: per-session token cost dashboard, checkpoint hit-rate metric, avg latency with/without checkpoint
- Run production A/B for 2 weeks: metric targets: checkpoint hit-rate > 75% for active sessions; token-per-turn reduction >= 40% for long sessions

Testing guidance and sample tests:
- Unit: session.restore returns expected metadata when checkpoint mocked
- Integration: simulate 50 concurrent sessions with 20-turn depth, measure median latency improvement when checkpointing enabled
- Regression: test that when system instruction changes, a forced full-prefix call creates a new checkpoint_id

Open questions / TODOs:
- Does Redwood runtime already guarantee deterministic rehydrate ordering when a checkpoint + short prefix are sent? We should confirm (ENG-serving-runtime).
- Where should we expose checkpoint size warnings to the user (SDK logs vs console)?
- Should the SDK offer an option to auto-compact checkpoints (strip high-entropy sequences) to stay under size limits? Implementation complexity vs user surprise.

Implementation notes for SDK engineers:
- Keep checkpoint blob opaque; runtime should validate and reject if incompatible
- Heartbeat pattern: if session active and last_turn < 2m, extend checkpoint TTL asynchronously
- Backoff strategy when rehydration fails: exponential backoff up to 5 retries then fall back to full-prefix path

Appendix: short prompt set for QA (use these to validate semantics)
- "You are a travel assistant. Remember the user likes boutique hostels and dislikes chains."
- "User earlier said they prefer hiking over museums — use that when suggesting activities."

Slack threads / references to link for follow-up:
- #eng-sdk (ping Samir about checkpoint telemetry format)
- #serving-runtime (confirm deterministic rehydrate ordering)

Quick notes to self: keep primitives minimal; avoid exposing too many knobs in 1.0. Make migration smooth so product teams get immediate latency wins.

-- end of working draft --
